'''Detlef Weigel''' (born 1961 in [[Lower Saxony]], [[Germany]]) is a German American<ref name="s578">{{cite web | title=Detlef Weigel – NAS | website=NAS | url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/detlef-weigel-myzyfo/ | access-date=25 December 2024}}</ref> scientist working at the interface of developmental and evolutionary biology.

==Education==

Weigel was an undergraduate in [[biology]] and [[chemistry]] at the universities of [[Bielefeld]] and [[Cologne]]. In 1986, he graduated with a [[Diploma]] in [[biology]] for this thesis on [[Drosophila]] [[neurogenesis]] with the late José Campos-Ortega. In 1988, he moved to the [[Max Planck Institute for Developmental Biology]] in [[Tübingen]]. During his PhD work with {{ill|Herbert Jäckle|de}},<ref name="v197">{{cite web | title=Leopoldina: Neugewählte Mitglieder 2008 | url=https://www.leopoldina.org/fileadmin/redaktion/Publikationen/Mitgliederverzeichnisse/English/mitg2008.pdf | access-date=25 December 2024}}</ref> he discovered the founding member of an important class of transcription factors, the [[Forkhead]]/[[FOX proteins|FOX]] proteins.<ref name="pmid2566386">{{cite journal |vauthors=Weigel D, Jürgens G, Küttner F, Seifert E, Jäckle H | title = The homeotic gene fork head encodes a nuclear protein and is expressed in the terminal regions of the Drosophila embryo | journal = Cell | volume = 57 | issue = 4 | pages = 645–658 | year = 1989 | pmid = 2566386 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(89)90133-5 | s2cid = 12317967 | doi-access =free }}</ref><ref name="pmid2225060">{{cite journal |vauthors=Weigel D, Jäckle H | title = The fork head domain, a novel DNA-binding motif of eucaryotic transcription factors? | journal = Cell | volume = 63 | issue = 3 | pages = 455–456 | year = 1990 | pmid = 2225060 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(90)90439-L | s2cid = 1986657 }}</ref> In 1988, he graduated with a PhD ([[summa cum laude]]) from the [[University of Tübingen]].

==Career and research==
Weigel began to work with [[plants]] during his [[postdoctoral]] research with [[Elliot M. Meyerowitz]] at [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]], where he [[cloned]] the floral regulator ''[[LEAFY]]'' from ''[[Arabidopsis thaliana]]''.<ref name="pmid1350515">{{cite journal |vauthors=Weigel D, Alvarez J, Smyth DR, Yanofsky MF, Meyerowitz EM | title = LEAFY controls floral meristem identity in Arabidopsis | journal = Cell | volume = 69 | issue = 5 | pages = 843–859 | year = 1992 | pmid = 1350515 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(92)90295-N | title-link = Arabidopsis thaliana | doi-access = free }}</ref> From 1993 to 2002, he was an Assistant and then associate professor at the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]] in [[La Jolla]]. In 2002, he accepted an appointment as Scientific Member and Director at the [[Max Planck Institute for Developmental Biology]], where he founded the Department for [[Molecular Biology]]. He is also an [[adjunct professor]] at the [[Salk Institute]] and the [[University of Tübingen]]. In 2012, Weigel co-founded the plant [[bioinformatics]] startup company [[Computomics]] in Tübingen.
He is Co-Editor-in-Chief of [[eLife]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://elifesciences.org/about/people |title = Leadership team}}</ref>

During the 1990s, Weigel mostly studied the development of individual flowers and how the onset of flowering is regulated. His group made important discoveries in both areas. Together with Ove Nilsson, he demonstrated that transfer of the ''[[LEAFY]]'' gene from ''[[Arabidopsis thaliana]]'' to [[aspen]] trees was sufficient to reduce the time to flowering from years to months.<ref name="pmid7566146">{{cite journal |vauthors=Weigel D, Nilsson O | title = A developmental switch sufficient for flower initiation in diverse plants | journal = Nature | volume = 377 | issue = 6549 | pages = 495–500 | year = 1995 | pmid = 7566146 | doi = 10.1038/377495a0 | bibcode = 1995Natur.377..495W | s2cid = 4346606 }}</ref> Weigel and his team isolated the ''FT'' gene,<ref name="pmid10583961">{{cite journal |vauthors=Kardailsky I, Shukla VK, Ahn JH, Dagenais N, Christensen SK, Nguyen JT, Chory J, Harrison MJ, Weigel D | title = Activation tagging of the floral inducer FT | journal = Science | volume = 286 | issue = 5446 | pages = 1962–1965 | year = 1999 | pmid = 10583961 | doi = 10.1126/science.286.5446.1962 }}</ref> which was later found to be an important component of the mobile signal inducing flowering.<ref name="pmid16099980">{{cite journal |vauthors=Wigge PA, Kim MC, Jaeger KE, Busch W, Schmid M, Lohmann JU, Weigel D | title = Integration of spatial and temporal information during floral induction in Arabidopsis | journal = Science | volume = 309 | issue = 5737 | pages = 1056–1059 | year = 2005 | pmid = 16099980 | doi = 10.1126/science.1114358 | bibcode = 2005Sci...309.1056W | s2cid = 20425470 }}</ref> New genetic tools developed by his group led to the discovery of the first [[microRNA]] mutant in plants.<ref name="pmid12931144">{{cite journal |vauthors=Palatnik JF, Allen E, Wu X, Schommer C, Schwab R, Carrington JC, Weigel D | title = Control of leaf morphogenesis by microRNAs | journal = Nature | volume = 425 | issue = 6955 | pages = 257–263 | year = 2003 | pmid = 12931144 | doi = 10.1038/nature01958 | url = http://edoc.mpg.de/47023 | bibcode = 2003Natur.425..257P | s2cid = 992057 | url-access = subscription }}</ref>

Through his study of factors that control the onset of flowering, a quintessential adaptive trait, Weigel became interested in more general questions of [[evolution]]. Apart from work on genetic variation in environment-dependent developmental processes, his group is known for the generation of extensive genomic resources, such as the first [[haplotype map]] for a non-mammalian species.<ref name="pmid176411934">{{cite journal |vauthors=Clark RM, Schweikert G, Toomajian C, Ossowski S, Zeller G, Shinn P, Warthmann N, Hu TT, Fu G, Hinds DA, Chen H, Frazer KA, Huson DH, Schölkopf B, Nordborg M, Rätsch G, Ecker JR, Weigel D | title = Common sequence polymorphisms shaping genetic diversity in ''Arabidopsis thaliana'' | journal = Science | volume = 317 | issue = 5836 | pages = 338–342 | year = 2007 | pmid = 17641193 | doi = 10.1126/science.1138632 | bibcode = 2007Sci...317..338C | s2cid = 39874240 }}</ref><ref name="pmid17676040">{{cite journal |vauthors=Kim S, Plagnol V, Hu TT, Toomajian C, Clark RM, Ossowski S, Ecker JR, Weigel D, Nordborg M | title = Recombination and linkage disequilibrium in ''Arabidopsis thaliana'' | journal = Nat. Genet. | volume = 39 | issue = 9 | pages = 1151–1155 | year = 2007 | pmid = 17676040 | doi = 10.1038/ng2115 | s2cid = 31681171 }}</ref> To further exploit and advance the understanding of genetic variation, Weigel and colleagues initiated the [http://1001genomes.org 1001 Genomes] project for ''[[Arabidopsis thaliana]]''. Related to this is a new area of interest, in genetic barriers. In collaboration with [[Jeffery Dangl]], his group discovered that such barriers in plants are often associated with [[autoimmunity]]. They could show that in certain [[hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] offspring, specific gene products contributed by one of the parents may be inappropriately recognized as foreign and pathogenic, and thus trigger pervasive cell death throughout the plant.<ref name="pmid17803357">{{cite journal |vauthors=Bomblies K, Lempe J, Epple P, Warthmann N, Lanz C, Dangl JL, Weigel D | title = Autoimmune response as a mechanism for a Dobzhansky-Muller-type incompatibility syndrome in plants | journal = PLOS Biol. | volume = 5 | issue = 9 | pages = e23 | year = 2007 | pmid = 17803357 | pmc = 1964774 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pbio.0050236 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Most of the causal genes encode components of the immune system, indicating that there are constraints on the assembly of an optimal immune system.<ref name="pmid25467443">{{cite journal |vauthors=Chae E, Bomblies K, Kim ST, Karelina D, Zaidem M, Ossowski S, Martín-Pizarro C, Laitinen RA, Rowan BA, Tenenboim H, Lechner S, Demar M, Habring-Müller A, Lanz C, Rätsch G, Weigel D | title = Species-wide genetic incompatibility analysis identifies immune genes as hot spots of deleterious epistasis | journal = Cell | volume = 159 | issue = 6 | pages = 1341–1351 | year = 2014 | pmid = 25467443 | pmc = 4269942 | doi = 10.1016/j.cell.2014.10.049}}</ref> Several cases have been examined in detail and shown to be due to direct protein-protein interactions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tran|first1=Diep ===Honors and awards===

*1989 Dieter Rampacher Award of the [[Max Planck Society]]
*1994 Young Investigator Award of the [[National Science Foundation]]
*2001 Charles Albert Shull Award of the [[American Society of Plant Biologists]]
*2003 Member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]] (EMBO)
*2007 [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize]] of the [[Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft]] (DFG)<ref name="a319">{{cite web | title=Leibniz-Preis | website=Max-Planck-Gesellschaft zur Förderung der Wissenschaften | date=4 November 2024 | url=https://www.mpg.de/Leibniz-Preis | language=de | access-date=25 December 2024}}</ref>
*2008 Member of the [[German Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]]
*2009 Member of the US [[National Academy of Sciences]]
*2010 [[Otto Bayer Award]] of the Bayer Foundations
*2010 [[Foreign Member of the Royal Society]]
*2011 Fellow, [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]
*2011 State Research Prize of Baden-Württemberg
*2015 Mendel Medal of the German National [[Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]]
*2016 [[Genetics Society of America Medal]]
*2019 [[McClintock Prize]]<ref name=mcprize>{{cite web|url=https://www.mpg.de/11985792/barbara-mcclintock-prize-2019-weigel|title=Detlef Weigel will receive the Barbara McClintock Prize 2019|website=www.mpg.de}}</ref>
*2019 Member of [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]
*2020 [[Novozymes Prize]] of the [[Novo Nordisk Foundation]]
